extracted.intended_audience: general readers, media researchers, and creators interested in television satire and The Daily Show
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative principles for producing or assessing late-night satirical/news-parody television (as exemplified by The Daily Show). Covers targets, tone, format, audience assumptions, journalistic expectations, and measures of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeting power
rubrics_metrics.description: "I think we consider those with power and influence targets and those without it, not."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer punching up: focus satire on people and institutions with real power or influence rather than marginalized or powerless targets. Examples in text: Colbert/Stewart remarks that making fun of Democrats when they lack power is like 'kicking a child'; Stewart targeted politicians for failing to stand effectively on issues. Anti-pattern: 'punching down' at those without power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principal goal is comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Ben Karlin: the principal goal of the show is comedy — "If you have a legitimately funny joke in support of the notion that gay people are an affront to God, we'll put that motherfucker on!"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial decisions prioritize comedic value over ideological consistency or political messaging. A joke's funniness can trump concerns about whether it aligns with a particular viewpoint; comedic payoff is the primary production criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground satire in truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Bloggers argue that 'so long as Stewart's comedy is grounded in truth, responsibility for increased cynicism belongs to the political and media figures themselves, not the comedian who satirizes them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire should be anchored in factual realities to maintain credibility and avoid undue misinformation. Grounding jokes in truth helps justify critical or cynical takes and is used as a defense against charges of irresponsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance satire and journalistic rigor in interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Stewart rejects being held to journalistic standards but has been criticized (e.g., by Lizz Winstead and Tucker Carlson) for not pressing guests hard enough in interviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hosts must navigate between comedic interview style and substantive challenge: do not let access or comic rapport prevent asking substantive, critical questions when appropriate. Anti-pattern: giving serious guests a free pass for the sake of access or comfort; pro-pattern: sometimes conducting hard-hitting interviews while remaining a comedy program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume an informed audience
rubrics_metrics.description: "Our show would not be valuable to people who didn't understand the news because it wouldn't make sense... We make assumptions about your level of knowledge..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content should presuppose some baseline of viewers' knowledge about current events; jokes often rely on prior awareness and context. Craft segments so they reward an audience already familiar with the news rather than educating from first principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondents' dual roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Correspondents function as satirical 'experts' with senior-sounding titles and as hosts of field-reporting segments offering humorous commentary and interviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correspondents should contribute to writing and development of their segments, perform both scripted and improvised material, and may serve as incubators for comedic talent. Examples: on-air talent are involved early in writing or add improv during rehearsal; the show has launched many careers (Carell, Colbert, Oliver, Bee, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearly label as parody when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: When aired on CNN International the broadcast was prefaced by a written disclaimer: 'The show you are about to watch is a news parody. Its stories are not fact checked. Its reporters are not journalists. And its opinions are not fully thought through.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For international syndication or in contexts where parody might be mistaken for straight news, include explicit disclaimers to prevent confusion. This is both an editorial and legal/ethical best practice for news-parody programming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential for political impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Stewart dedicated an entire episode to the James Zadroga 9/11 Health and Compensation Act, helping revive the bill; commentators praised Stewart for influencing its passage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers should recognize the real-world influence such programs can exert; careful, sustained coverage of an issue can galvanize public attention and political action. Use this power responsibly, especially when spotlighting under-covered matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt format under constraints while maintaining integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: During the 2007–08 writers' strike the show returned ad-libbed without writers and temporarily titled itself 'A Daily Show...' in solidarity; during COVID-19 the show produced at-home webisodes and later preserved elements of intimacy when returning to studio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When faced with production, labor, or public-health constraints, adapt delivery (remote production, altered runtime, different titling) but preserve core creative and ethical elements (tone, solidarity with writers, audience relationship). Respect labor rules (e.g., guild restrictions on writing) and find compliant ways to continue output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Host voice and demographic targeting
rubrics_metrics.description: Trevor Noah implemented stylistic changes (new set, graphics, standing monologues, Millennial references, impersonations) to reflect his younger demographic and multilingual skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A host's personal style and cultural background should shape tone, references, and segment structure to connect with target demographics. Programming and content must be tuned to audience tastes while retaining the show's satirical mission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve core show elements through format changes
rubrics_metrics.description: When the show expanded to 45 minutes and temporarily used at-home formats, Comedy Central said it aimed to 'preserve the intimacy and creative elements' of the home-based episodes upon returning to studio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even with changes in length, platform, or production location, retain defining characteristics (intimacy, pacing, recurring segments) so the show's identity and audience relationship remain intact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure success across multiple metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: The article lists Nielsen ratings, demographic composition (younger, well-educated skew), Facebook likes/geographic popularity, awards (Peabody, Emmys), and influence as markers of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a satirical news program both by traditional audience metrics (ratings, demographic reach), digital engagement, critical recognition (awards, citations), and demonstrable cultural/political impact. Different stakeholders will weight these metrics differently (advertisers, critics, producers).
